label: G.657.A2 drop 4F
notes: Four fibres, tight-buffered flat drop in one tube, so the strands address as T01-F01 blue, F02 orange, F03 green, F04 brown per TIA-598 - one cable to a four-port tap instead of two g657a2-drop-2 runs down the same span. Why the rung exists: the drop family stopped at two fibres and the next size up in this catalogue is twelve (g657a2-indoor-12, an indoor riser), so the only four-fibre cable a short span could name was g652d-loose-12 - twelve fibres of gel-filled outdoor loose tube to light four. This row is that missing rung. What it does, measured on this engine rather than assumed: engine/design.js's cableForSpan gives a span at or below DROP_CABLE_MAX_M (300 m) the smallest rung of the caller's ladder that carries its fibres and that the catalogue calls a drop (use: ["drop"]), at any fibre count - so when the design's ladder names this row, a three- or four-fibre short span is billed four-fibre drop, not twelve fibres of gel-filled outdoor loose tube (gh#144, test/design-drop-cable-above-two.test.js and test/design-drop-cable-catalogue.test.js). Measured: cableForSpan(4, 100, ['g652d-loose-12', 'g657a2-drop-4', 'g657a2-drop-2', 'g657a2-drop-1']) answers g657a2-drop-4, while cableForSpan(4, 301, ...) and any longer run answer g652d-loose-12 - over 300 m a span is a cable run, not a drop, and the 12-fibre floor applies. DEFAULT_LADDER does not name this row: cableForSpan(4, 100, DEFAULT_LADDER) answers g652d-loose-12, so a planner who supplies no ladder still buys 12F on a short 3-4 fibre span. Whether the rung belongs on DEFAULT_LADDER is a separate decision, because it re-ranks auto-design candidates rather than moving one span's cable - measured on the 12-house estate it changes the winner from PON 1:8 (9,410.4 purchased fibre-metres) to PON 1:16 (8,009.3) - and it is tracked in gh#155. Until that decision, this rung is reached by naming it in the design's ladder or on the span (cable). Attenuation is the same typical installed row every drop, feeder and indoor cable here carries (0.35 / 0.22 / 0.21 dB/km), and deliberately so: G.657.A2 publishes the same attenuation maxima as G.652.D - 0.40 dB/km over 1310-1625 nm and 0.30 dB/km over 1530-1565 nm - so the two families do not differ in attenuation and one row is justified. 0.35 sits under the first maximum and 0.21 under the second; 1490 nm is a typical, interpolated value, because neither the ITU-T recommendation nor any sheet this catalogue cites publishes a 1490 nm figure, so 0.22 is not a citation. All three are typical installed performance, not a limit, and must be replaced with the purchased cable's test report before construction. What the row does not buy is bend loss in the budget: G.657.A2 allows 0.1 dB for one turn at 10 mm radius at 1550 nm (0.5 dB at 7.5 mm) and this catalogue budgets no macrobend at all, so the grade only helps if the crew holds the radius. 1000 m is a flat-drop putup, not a standard - 500 to 2000 m reels are sold - so replace drumM with the putup of the cable actually ordered.
